I. 
INTRODUCTION 
1. 
By this Order,1 the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia 
(“Commission”) grants the request of Trane Energy Choice, LLC (“TEC” or “Applicant”), 
formerly Global Energy Market Services, LLC (“GEMS”) to surrender its electricity supplier 
license. Cancellation of the Applicant’s electricity supplier license is effective upon the issuance

GEMS filed notice of a change in name to TEC, the name under which it operates today.3 On June

III. 
DISCUSSION 

3. 
According to 15 DCMR § 4602.10 (a)(1), a licensed electricity supplier wishing to 
cease providing services in the District is required to provide written notice to the Commission of 
the licensee’s intention to cease providing electricity service to its customers and inform its 
customers of the choice to revert to the default service provider or another electricity supplier. 
Section 4602.10 (a)(2) also requires that the surrendering licensee provide to the Commission an 
example or copy of the notice it provided to its customers and, upon the Commission’s receipt of 
such notice, may order the licensee to provide such further notice to its customers or the public as 
the Commission deems necessary, and/or take such other action that the Commission considers 
appropriate.7 

4. 
In the instant case, TEC’s Application provides the required notice to the 
Commission of its intention to surrender its electricity supplier license.8 TEC also states that the 
notice requirement to customers is inapplicable because it has no customers in the District.9 
Accordingly, TEC’s Application satisfies the notice requirement with regard to the cessation of 
service. 

5. 
In all other respects, TEC’s Application substantially conforms with Commission 
requirements for a surrendering licensee. Commission records confirm the Applicant’s submission 
of the case number and date the Applicant’s license was granted.10 TEC avers, and Commission 
records confirm that the Applicant’s most recent survey response indicates no jurisdictional 
revenue and that it owes no outstanding debt or fees.11 In addition, the Applicant states that it has 
no outstanding consumer complaints.12 Lastly, the signed Application from an officer of TEC 
attests to the truth and accuracy of the information submitted.13

WASHINGTON, DC 20005

FORMAL CASE NO. 1125, IN THE MATTER OF THE PROMOTION OF THE UTILITY 
DISCOUNT PROGRAMS, Order No. 22897 

I. 
INTRODUCTION 

1. 
By this Order,1 the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia 
(“Commission”) approves the Utility Discount Program Education Working Group’s (“UDPE 
WG”) Consumer Education Program (“CEP”) Plan for Fiscal Year 2027 (“Proposed FY 2027 
CEP”).2 The Commission approves the CEP and the CEP administrative costs contained in the 
Proposed FY 2027 CEP, the Utility Discount Program (“UDP”) administrative budget, and the 
cost allocation among the District of Columbia Water and Sewer Authority (“DC Water”), the 
Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco”), and Washington Gas Light Company (“WGL”) for 
the UDP administrative budget as filed. The Commission directs the District Department of 
Energy and Environment (“DOEE”) to continue its monthly reports and to continue to provide the 
UDPE WG with a proposed UDP administrative budget and CEP budget for the next fiscal year 
by December 31, 2026. 

II. 
BACKGROUND 

2. 
In Order No. 16615, the Commission fundamentally changed the education and 
outreach program for low-income consumers to obtain information about and access to the four 
UDPs in the District of Columbia (“District”).3 Rather than hosting a single annual event—the 
Joint Utility Discount Day—to enroll eligible customers, the Commission approved the creation 
of a year-long CEP to continuously educate consumers about the utility discount programs through 
various media channels. Because the CEP operates on the District fiscal year calendar (October 1

III. 
DISCUSSION 

A. 
Proposed FY 2027 CEP and UDP Administrative Budget 

3. 
For FY 2027, the UDPE WG seeks to increase opportunities to facilitate program 
enrollment. The UDPE WG continues to emphasize social media, since social media 
advertisements can be tailored to appeal to all District residents but be specifically targeted to 
connect with residents of targeted zip codes and Wards. The UDPE WG contends that social 
media can help leverage the leading promotional tool for the UDP – word of mouth. The UDPE 
WG’s social media vendor also produces detailed quarterly reports showing measurable results 
and metrics.4 

4. 
The UDPE WG proposes some changes to the $100,000 CEP budget allocations. 
The proposed FY 2027 CEP includes: $10,000 for radio advertisements; $20,000 for Washington 
Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (“WMATA”) advertisements; $50,000 for Social Driver, the 
administrator for the CEP social media presence; and $5,000 each for print newspapers El Tiempo 
Latino, Capital Community Newspapers, the Blade, and the Beacon. The UDPE WG indicates that 
UDP advertisements will run on five of Urban One’s stations. The UDPE WG proposes to increase 
the radio budget to be able to purchase advertisements for the new radio show hosted by Russ Parr, 
a popular radio announcer. WMATA advertisements will be placed on local buses, particularly in 
Wards 5, 7, and 8. Banner advertisements at specific Metrorail stations will be added.5 The UDPE 
WG represents that Social Driver will assist with advertisements on Facebook, Twitter (X), and 
Instagram to boost program awareness, drive website traffic, and encourage audience participation 
and engagement.6 The UDPE WG selected El Tiempo to run Spanish UDP advertisements. 
Additional print advertisements will be placed in Capital Community News, a returning vendor as 
well as the Washington Blade and the Beacon, which will be added in FY 2027.7 The UDPE WG 
is continuing to search for a vendor for the Amharic-speaking community.8 Free advertisements 
will continue to run on the District Government’s community cable channels.9

promote the UDP. OCS will also distribute information flyers in multiple languages. OCS will 
also analyze pertinent metrics.15

UDP on its website. DOEE will also partner with the Mayor’s Office on Latino Affairs, the 
Mayor’s Office on African Affairs, and the Mayor’s Office on Asians and Pacific Islanders to

first three quarters of the year, DOEE will file invoices within 30 days of the end of the quarter,

IV. 
DECISION 

19.

participation in RES and RAD increased to 80% of the area median income to incentivize greater

UDPE WG to enhance awareness and accessibility of the four UDPs for current and potential

A. 
Proposed FY 2027 CEP 

20.

its focus on innovative social media campaigns, ensuring more immediate and measurable 
feedback on outreach effectiveness. The UDPE WG asserts that the social media advertisements

description: The Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia, in Formal Case No. 1102, by Order No. 22896, dated July 2, 2026, closed this proceeding. The purpose of this matter was to investigate issues relating to the use of Verizon Washington, DC Inc.’s (“Verizon DC”) copper infrastructure for the provision of telecommunications services. By the end of 2023, Verizon DC replaced all copper distribution and loop facilities with fiber-to-the-premises facilities at all locations in the District of Columbia. permissible only where the underlying rates have been found to be substantively unlawful, such as 
unjust, unreasonable, confiscatory, or otherwise invalid on their merits. Here, the Court identified 
a procedural defect in the Commission’s prior order and expressly found the existing rates to be 
unlawful. Order No. 22860 also noted that decisions such as Potomac Electric Power Co. v. PSC 
(1977) and District of Columbia v. PSC (2006) confirm that refunds are appropriate only when 
rates themselves have been determined to be unlawful.206 Because the Court made no such finding 
here, but instead vacated Order No. 22328 for lack of an evidentiary hearing and insufficient 
explanation, refunds are not available. Nothing in Baker alters this conclusion. Baker involved an 
appellate determination that the underlying rate treatment was unlawful on its merits. In this case, 
the Court did not make any such finding. Because the Court vacated Order No. 22328 solely for 
lack of an evidentiary hearing and fuller explanation, and not because the resulting rates were 
improper, the legal predicate for ordering refunds is absent. OPC’s refund claim, therefore, 
provides no basis for reconsideration. With respect to OPC’s assertion of a constitutional property 
interest in retroactive refunds, the Commission finds no due process violation. A property interest 
arises only when an individual has a legitimate claim of entitlement, not a unilateral expectation,

to a specific remedy.207 In the absence of a judicial or Commission finding that the existing rates

OPC contends that the Commission erred by limiting the scope of the remand and

Commission to rebuild the evidentiary record necessary to adjudicate the issues the Court 
identified and to base any 2026 projections on verified recent data. The mere passage of time does 
not render the MRP obsolete, nor does it prevent the Commission from completing the adjudication 
required on remand. The prohibition on retroactive ratemaking does not bar the use of updated 
actuals to inform prospective rate determinations; rather, it ensures that approved rates apply only 
prospectively. Updated actuals and refreshed testimony serve that purpose by supplying the 
evidentiary foundation necessary to support a Commission decision. Because the Court did not 
require dismissal of the MRP, and because the Commission can lawfully evaluate the MRP using 
current, verified data without violating retroactive ratemaking principles, OPC’s mootness theory 
identifies no error in Order No. 22860 and provides no basis for reconsideration.

regulatory stability, avoid administrative disruption, and protect ratepayers from uncertainty.210 
The interim rate posture is not a merits determination; it does not prejudge any issue concerning 
the justness or reasonableness of Pepco’s rates. All prudency, cost‑variance, rate‑design, and

litigated and resolved based on the evidentiary record developed during the remand process, to 
include the evidentiary hearing. Because the interim rate decision preserves stability while the 
Commission undertakes the evidentiary hearing required by the Court, OPC’s newly raised

10. OPC’s Baker‑Based Refund Theory Provides No Basis for Reconsideration 

77. 
OPC also advances an expanded set of arguments relying on Washington Gas Light 
Co. v. Baker, asserting that refunds are warranted even absent a finding of substantive 
unlawfulness, that Baker applies to procedural vacatur, and that refunds may be ordered while 
remand proceedings are still pending. This newly raised theory was not raised prior to OPC’s 
Application for Reconsideration, and accordingly, Order No. 22860 did not address it. The

hearing and an insufficient explanation) and made no finding that the resulting rates were unjust, 
unreasonable, confiscatory, or otherwise unlawful. As Order No. 22860 already explained, refunds

reaffirmed in decisions such as Potomac Electric Power Co. v. PSC and District of Columbia v.

Baker‑based theory, therefore, identifies no error in Order No. 22860 and does not provide a basis

78.

constitute a protected property interest under the Fourteenth Amendment and that continued 
collection of current rates amounts to an ongoing deprivation. Because no party previously raised 
such a constitutional claim, Order No. 22860 did not address this new theory. The Commission

the financial pressures faced by District households are serious matters, and it does not discount 
OPC’s concerns. Nevertheless, OPC’s constitutional framing does not alter the governing legal

otherwise improper. Instead, it identified a procedural defect, specifically, the absence of an 
evidentiary hearing and the need for fuller explanation, and remanded the matter for further 
proceedings. Under established District law, a refund obligation arises only when rates themselves 
have been found substantively unlawful. Without such a determination by either the Court or the 
Commission, there is no legally cognizable property interest in retroactive refunds that would 
trigger a Fourteenth Amendment deprivation. Maintaining the currently effective tariffed rates 
during the remand period pending completion of the evidentiary hearing required by the Court 
does not constitute a due process violation. Accordingly, while the Commission remains attentive

and develops the full record necessary to address all prudency, cost‑variance, and rate‑design

administratively workable and fairly applied to all affected customers, including those who may 
relocate during the pendency of the remand. However, the legal predicate for refunds remains 
unchanged. Under long‑standing District precedent, refunds may be ordered only when the 
underlying rates have been found substantively unlawful; here, the Court identified a procedural 
deficiency but made no determination that the existing rates are unjust, unreasonable, or otherwise 
invalid. Because no such finding has been made, the question of refund administration does not 
arise at this stage. Concerns regarding customer mobility and refund logistics, while important to 
consider in appropriate circumstances, do not establish any error in Order No. 22860 and do not

Factual Findings Do Not Support Reconsideration 

81. 
OPC further contends that the MRP has become “purely academic” under the 
judicial mootness doctrine, arguing that the issues presented are no longer live and that the 
Commission cannot provide effective relief. This newly expanded mootness theory was not raised 
before OPC’s Application for Reconsideration, and as a result, Order No. 22860 did not address 
this argument. The Commission finds OPC’s mootness theory unpersuasive because the issues 
remain live and the Commission can still provide effective relief through its remand determination. 
The Court did not hold that the issues presented in this proceeding are moot, nor did it direct the 
Commission to dismiss the MRP. To the contrary, the Court remanded the matter for the 
Commission to conduct the evidentiary hearing previously omitted and to provide additional 
explanation of specific determinations. A controversy plainly remains: the justness and 
reasonableness of Pepco’s rates for the remand period must still be adjudicated on a full evidentiary 
record, and the Commission retains the authority to modify those rates based on the outcome of 
that hearing. Moreover, the Commission has already directed Pepco to submit updated actual 
expenditure data for 2024–2025 and supplemental testimony on prudency, cost variances, and 
ERA/BSA mechanics, ensuring that the remand proceeding will produce a current and complete 
evidentiary record capable of supporting effective prospective relief. The judicial mootness 
doctrine does not apply where, as here, meaningful relief remains available, and the Commission 
is engaged in the adjudicatory process required by the Court. 

82. 
OPC additionally argues that the MRP cannot lawfully be adjudicated on remand 
because, in OPC’s view, Order Nos. 22328 and 22358, and the MRP they approved was vacated 
in its entirety, leaving no proper factual findings. OPC asserts that the absence of prior factual 
findings means the Commission “cannot supplement a plan devoid of factual findings” and that, 
because the forecasts underlying Pepco’s original filing have since been overtaken by actuals, the 
core justiciable issues are now obsolete. The Commission finds OPC’s argument unpersuasive and 
inconsistent with both the Vacatur Decision and the governing statutory framework. First, the 
Court did not hold that the absence of prior factual findings renders the MRP incapable of 
adjudication, nor did it direct the Commission to dismiss the MRP Application. Instead, the Court 
expressly remanded the matter for the Commission to conduct the evidentiary hearing and to 
provide a fuller explanation of specific determinations. A remand to conduct an evidentiary 
hearing necessarily presumes that the Commission must now create the evidentiary record that was 
previously lacking, including making the factual findings required to support whatever rate 
determinations are ultimately made. The absence of prior factual findings is precisely the 
procedural defect the remand is designed to cure, not a basis for dismissal. Second, OPC’s assertion 
that the MRP cannot be supplemented because its forecasts have grown stale misstates both the 
purpose and operation of a remand. As Order No. 22860 explained, the Court did not invalidate 
the MRP framework. Consistent with the remand directive, the Commission has required Pepco to 
file updated actual expenditure data for 2024–2025, along with supplemental testimony addressing 
prudency, cost variances, and the mechanics of the ERA and BSA. These updated data will enable 
the Commission to rebuild the evidentiary record using verified information, ensuring that any 
prospective rate determination rests on substantial, current evidence. The rule against retroactive 
ratemaking does not bar the use of updated actuals to inform prospective ratemaking; it merely 
prohibits retroactive adjustment of previously collected revenues. Third, OPC’s argument that the 

Order No. 22892 

Page No. 33 

MRP must be dismissed because its original forecasts pertained to years that have substantially 
passed is inconsistent with the Court’s mandate and unsupported by District law. The Court did 
not hold that passage of time moots a rate application on remand. Nor does the D.C. Code forbid 
the Commission from adjudicating a partially elapsed multiyear plan where the evidentiary record 
is reconstructed using verified, updated information. The Commission’s process of requiring 
updated actuals, supplemental testimony, and an evidentiary hearing is tailored to produce the 
complete factual record necessary to support the Commission’s decision on remand. Nothing 
prevents the Commission from making prospective determinations based on current data while 
evaluating the MRP framework that the Court left intact. Accordingly, OPC’s newly asserted 
mootness theory and the absence of prior factual findings or the passage of forecast years render 
the MRP incapable of adjudication, do not identify any error in Order No. 22860, and do not 
provide a basis for reconsideration. 

83. 
After careful review of OPC’s Application for Reconsideration, the Commission 
finds that OPC has not demonstrated any error of law or fact in Order No. 22860, nor has it 
identified any circumstance warranting the extraordinary remedy of reconsideration. The majority 
of OPC’s arguments repeat positions the Commission has previously considered and rejected. The 
Vacatur Decision was expressly procedural and did not invalidate the MRP framework, the 
existing tariffed rates, or the Commission’s authority to maintain those rates during remand. The 
Court did not order reinstatement of prior rates, mandate refunds, or otherwise disturb the 
Commission’s ratemaking responsibilities. The Commission has already taken significant steps to 
implement the Court’s directive by requiring updated actuals, supplemental testimony, and a full 
evidentiary hearing capable of producing the complete factual record the Court found lacking. The 
Commission remains mindful of its statutory obligations to ensure just and reasonable rates, to 
consider the economic realities faced by District residents, and to maintain transparency and 
fairness throughout the remand proceeding. Nothing in OPC’s Application undermines the 
Commission’s conclusions in Order No. 22860 or the remand process now underway. 
Accordingly, and consistent with the governing legal standards, the Commission reaffirms its 
determinations in Order No. 22860 and denies OPC’s Application for Reconsideration.

Prospectivity. 

84.

reaffirms that refunds are inappropriate only where there has been no court reversal or vacatur of 
the underlying Commission order.213 OPC further contends that the Court’s reliance on United Gas 
Improvement Co. v. Callery Properties, Inc., 382 U.S. 223, 229 (1965), confirms that even if an 
administrative agency lacks independent authority to order reparations, it may nevertheless 
implement remedies necessary to effectuate a judicial reversal, especially when failing to do so 
would, in OPC’s opinion, violate the filed rate doctrine and the prohibition against retroactive 
ratemaking. Pepco, on the other hand, argues that giving notice that a rate is subject to future 
adjustment is functionally prospective and creates an exception to both retroactive ratemaking and

INTRODUCTION
1.
By this Order, the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia
(“Commission”) grants the Office of People’s Counsel for the District of Columbia’s (“OPC”) 
motion for status and holds in abeyance the OPC petition to establish an Independent Distribution 
Monitor (“IDM”) to evaluate and oversee Washington Gas Light Company’s (“WGL” or

(“District”). WGL is directed to hold the last series of technical conferences on leak mapping and 
Geospatial Information Systems (“GIS”) in Formal Case No. 1178 within 45 days of the date of

Commission. This Order also directs WGL and stakeholders to file a joint report in Formal Case 
No. 1178 within 180 days of the date of this Order.

fulfill procedural prerequisites by concluding technical conferences within Formal Case Nos. 977 
and 1178 and submit joint, formal recommendations for natural gas distribution system monitoring 
as described herein. Accordingly, the Commission directs WGL and stakeholders to complete the

LIDAROC reporting. The Commission expects to use the discussions held in the Formal Case

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA

I.
INTRODUCTION
1.
This matter is an appeal from a Hearing Officer decision dismissing a
consumer complaint filed by Rebecca Levinson (“Complainant” or “Ms. Levinson”) 
against the Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco” or “Company”).1 By this Order, 
the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia (“Commission”) affirms the 
Dismissal Order of the Hearing Officer and denies the Appeal. 
II.
BACKGROUND
2.
The following facts are undisputed. Complainant installed a photovoltaic
system on her home and uses a solar energy generation app to monitor and manage what 
her system is doing. In July 2024, Pepco granted Complainant authorization to connect 
her system to the energy grid, which allows her to participate in net metering and receive 
a credit for the solar generated energy she produces in excess of the grid energy that she 
consumes. That same month, Complainant advised Pepco that she didn’t think Pepco’s 
system was properly crediting her for generation. Pepco investigated the matter and 
discovered a system communication error, which Pepco corrected in August 2024. 
3.
In October 2024, Pepco discovered another system error that resulted in
Complainant being underbilled for consumption and revised her bills. The revised billing 
included a calculation that Complainant’s excess kWh generation balance through 
October 23, 2024, to be 145 kWh. However, upon further investigation, Pepco 
discovered yet another error, this one caused the daily register readings for her generation 
to be undercounted by a factor of ten. Therefore, in December 2024, Pepco revised 
Complainant’s billing to reflect an upward adjustment of generation from 145 kWh to 
1,449 kWh. 
4.
Complainant wasn’t convinced that Pepco had properly credited her

generation so, in February 2025, she filed a complaint with the Commission demanding 
that Pepco provide her with a detailed accounting of her bills. In response, Pepco 
acknowledged its mistakes and explained that part of the confusion is that Complainant is 
trying to be credited for energy that she generated before being authorized to connect to 
the grid. Although Pepco says that energy generated before approval to connect to the 
grid is not subject to credit under its NEM tariff, as a gesture of goodwill, Pepco said that 
it would credit her for an additional 19 kWh. Unfortunately, a ‘scrivener’s error’ recorded 
the credit as 19,000 kWh, creating another mistake that Pepco had to correct. Even so, 
Pepco said that it had corrected all its mistakes and adjusted the billing accordingly so 
there’s no relief left for the Commission’s Hearing Officer to give. 

5. 
Complainant continued to believe that she was not properly billed. As the 
matter was still before the Hearing Officer for the 2025 summer billing cycle, 
Complainant suggested using the 2025 billing data in place of data for 2024 on the theory 
that the same calendar months one year apart represent comparable usage. The Hearing 
Officer found no legal basis for this proposal, especially since Pepco had provided him 
with actual data for the period at issue. Having reviewed all of Complainant’s arguments, 
the Hearing Officer found that she had not met her burden of proving that she was 
entitled to more than Pepco had given her and dismissed the case. This appeal followed.2 

III. 
DISCUSSION 

6. 
Complainant is understandably dissatisfied with a billing process riddled 
with errors. However, we agree with the Hearing Officer that Complainant has not 
proved entitlement to more relief than Pepco has already given her. We, therefore, affirm 
the Hearing Officer’s Order and deny the Complainant’s Appeal. 

THEREFORE, IT IS ORDERED THAT: 

7. 
Based on the foregoing, the Dismissal Order of the Hearing Officer is 
AFFIRMED; and 

8. 
The Complainant’s Objection, Exceptions, and Petition for Review of 
Order Dismissing Formal Hearing Complaint is DENIED.

TES requests to surrender its natural gas supplier license.5

III. 
DISCUSSION 

3. 
According to 15 DCMR § 4702.10 (a)(1), a licensed natural gas supplier wishing 
to cease providing services in the District is required to provide written notice to the Commission 
of the licensee’s intention to cease providing natural gas service to its customers and inform its 
customers of the choice to revert to the default service provider or another natural gas supplier. 
Section 4702.10 (a)(2) also requires that the surrendering licensee provide to the Commission an 
example or copy of the notice provided to its customers and, upon the Commission’s receipt of 
such notice, may order the licensee to provide such further notice to its customers or the public as 
the Commission deems necessary, and/or take such other action that the Commission considers

5.

Applicant’s most recent survey response indicates no jurisdictional revenue and that it owes no

the truth and accuracy of the information submitted.12 

6.

surrender its natural gas supplier license granted by Order No. 18522. Cancellation of TES’s
